author: ASHLEY RODRIGUEZ Keys
title: Ethics commission dismisses Kaufman's complaint against mayor and city manager - NewsBreak
text:
By ASHLEY RODRIGUEZ Keys ,
13 hours ago
The Florida Commission on Ethics dismissed ethics complaints filed by City Commissioner Sam Kaufman against City Manager Brian L. Barroso and Mayor Danise “Dee Dee” Henriquez.
Both complaints alleged that city resources and city-operated social media accounts were used to benefit Henriquez’s reelection campaign. The commission ruled a lack of legal sufficiency.
The complaints were filed in June by mayoral candidate Kaufman, alleging that city-operated social media accounts and communication platforms have been used to disproportionately promote Henriquez and benefit her reelection campaign while excluding or minimizing other elected officials. He said he had identified approximately 150 city-produced social media posts and communications that he believes demonstrate a pattern of preferential treatment.
The complaints followed a separate dispute between Kaufman and Barroso over a Dec. 26, 2025, incident in which Barroso accused Kaufman of improperly accessing City Hall while it was closed for the holiday. Kaufman has disputed that allegation.
Among the examples cited is a city social media post promoting a Memorial Day weekend event that stated it was paid for by Henriquez’s political campaign. Kaufman also alleged that city-produced photographs and videos later appeared on Henriquez’s personal and campaign-related social media accounts.
Kaufman further alleged selective enforcement by city administration, arguing that Barroso publicly raised allegations against him regarding use of city facilities while no similar investigation or enforcement action has been taken regarding communications benefiting Henriquez.
In dismissal orders issued on July 29, the ethics commission ruled that allegations, even if accepted as true, did not amount to legally sufficient violation of state ethics law.
Both orders by the commission stress that the review was limited to legal sufficiency and that no factual investigation took place, meaning the dismissals “do not reflect on the accuracy of the allegations.”
The ethics commission’s order suggested that although Kaufman contends that under the City Charter that the City Manager is “responsible for ensuring that governmental communications systems and public resources are administered lawfully” that he failed to allege that Barroso “personally had anything to do with the posts at issue.”
The order dismissing his complaint against Henriquez also suggests that Kaufman failed to indicate a possible violation of Florida statute Section 112.313(6), that he referenced.
Regarding Kaufman’s allegations that Henriquez was being disproportionately featured in city communications, the order stated that there was no indication that Henriquez “has personally directed City staff to favor her in any way in that context.”
They also dismissed his claims about Henriquez’s role in the Memorial Day campaign post, suggesting there was no indication she played a role in their transmission. The commission referred to an email by city attorney Mayanne Downs, in response to a residents concerns, that was attached to Kaufman’s complaint.
“We have investigated the matter and determined the posts you flagged were not made by any [C]ity personnel and were not authorized by the City or its staff,” Downs wrote. “The available evidence indicates a cyber-security breach. Our IT department has confirmed that no [C]ity personnel with authority to post on the City’s behalf were signed in at the time the posts appeared.”
Regarding Kaufman’s allegations surrounding unequal enforcement of standards related to the use of public resources, the commission found that there is no indication that Henriquez directed the city manager to target Kaufman or that anyone personally connected to Barroso benefited from the alleged selective enforcement. The order suggested even if this was a detriment to Kaufman, from a legal standpoint, something has to be gained from it, which the complaint didn’t establish, according to the commission.
The order dismissing the complaint against Henriquez also suggested that there was no allegation that she directed the city to create social media content for personal campaign purposes and that she wrongfully obtained this media.
Henriquez and Barroso both made announcements regarding the ethics commission’s order.
Barroso addressed city commissioners and the mayor in an email, reflecting the language of the ethics commission’s conclusions.
“The report... notes that there was no indication that I was personally involved in the creation or dissemination of the social media posts at issue and references the City’s investigation as identifying the incident as a cybersecurity breach rather than an authorized City communication,” Barroso wrote.
His email also reflected his statements in May, indicating he intended to disclose the underlying dispute to the full commission.
“I wanted to provide this information to the [City] Commission as part of maintaining transparency and ensuring everyone has the official disposition of this matter.”
Henriquez took to her campaign’s social media page to address the dismissed ethics complaint.
“Throughout this campaign, accusations have been made, and political narratives have been pushed. Today, the official record speaks for itself,” she wrote.
In a statement provided by Kaufman, he stated he disagreed with the Ethics Commission’s decision.
“What stands out to me is that the Commission said it did not investigate the facts before dismissing the complaint,” Kaufman wrote. “It also referenced ongoing investigations by the Key West Police Department and the FBI, so those issues have not been resolved.”
“My concern has always been simple. The City’s communication channels, including its official social media pages, should never give one candidate an advantage over another. Whether that meets the legal definition of an ethics violation is one question. Whether it’s fair to the public is another.”
Kaufman reemphasized his concerns over the Memorial Day social media posts and the impact of the city’s social media posts impacting upcoming elections.
Henriquez and Barroso’s statements regarding the dismissals came out just one day before Thursday’s city commission meeting. As of Wednesday, the dismissals did not appear on the meeting’s posted agenda.
summary: The complaints were filed in June by mayoral candidate Kaufman, alleging that city-operated social media accounts and communication platforms have been used to disproportionately promote Henriquez and benefit her reelection campaign while excluding or minimizing other elected officials. Among the examples cited is a city social media post promoting a Memorial Day weekend event that stated it was paid for by Henriquez’s political campaign.
